svg.text: U.S. Unemployment
One headline rate hides several stories
Bureau of Labor Statistics data: race, age, state, education and the broader U-6 measure.
A Black–White gap that has held for 50 years
Black unemployment rate ÷ White unemployment rate, each year 1973–2026 (annual averages).
average ratio, 1973–2026
At or above 2-to-1 in 36 of 54 years; never below 1.5-to-1. Orange dots = 2× or more.
What the official rate leaves out
U-6 (adds discouraged workers and involuntary part-timers) minus the official U-3, in points.
official U-3, 2026
broad U-6, 2026
The gap widens in downturns (2001–03, 2008–10, 2020) and has run 3.0–7.1 points since 1994.
Teenagers carry several times the adult rate
Unemployment rate, teens 16–19 (orange) vs workers 20 and over (teal), each year 1948–2026.
teen ÷ adult rate in 2026 (14.0% vs 3.9%)
Ranges from 2.3× (2021) to 4.6× (1968); average 3.3×. Share of the labor force, not of all teens.
State by state, one stands out
Trailing-12-month unemployment rate for all 51 states and DC, ranked.
DC is the only place at or above 6%
lowest: SD
DC
SD
Median state: 4.2%. Wyoming has only 5 months of data in the trailing window.
More education doesn't close the gap
Unemployment rate by education, White (teal) vs Black (orange) workers, 2024. Right column = Black ÷ White.
A Black worker with a bachelor’s degree has the same rate as a White worker with some college.
Less than high school
High school, no college
Some college or associate degree
Bachelor's degree and higher
@unwelcomedata
BLS CPS & LAUS · seasonally adjusted · U-6 starts 1994 (CPS redesign); 2011 duration cap. Black/White ratio is mean of annual rates.
